title: Global Energy Cyber Threat Intelligence Report
provenance_note: Transcribed from the PDF text. The report's hyperlinked citations are recorded by name; the PDF text did not carry the URLs, so each source is 'to resolve' until the Archivist attaches the primary URL. The accompanying 95-record spreadsheet (59 direct energy, 15 supplier/dependency, 18 adjacent water, 3 cross-sector; 38 country labels) was not attached.

ledger.note: The request for 200 cases was deliberately not met by splitting campaigns, counting advisories as attacks, or adding physical incidents.

three_paths.path: IT compromise forcing an operational suspension
three_paths.controls: IT/OT separation; manual dispatch; recovery independent of IT

three_paths.path: Crossing into OT and using legitimate control interfaces or industrial protocols
three_paths.controls: protocol-aware monitoring; command authorization; independent local control

three_paths.path: Attacks on shared communications, identity, providers and remote management that remove view of distant assets
three_paths.example: Viasat KA-SAT 2022 and German wind turbines
three_paths.controls: dependency map; alternate telemetry; manual fallback

highest_confidence_concern: Exposed remote access, reusable credentials, vendor maintenance pathways and insufficiently monitored OT segments (Poland December 2025 as the reference case).

method.unit: a distinct observed operation against an energy entity or a clearly identified energy dependency; a coordinated campaign is one record even if several facilities were affected
source_rank: (1) victim disclosures, government incident reports, filings, responder forensic reports, court records
(2) reputable contemporaneous reporting with named sources
(3) curated databases (EuRepoC, The Observatory) for discovery and triangulation only

attribution_tiers.confirmed: legal attribution, acknowledged responsibility, or unusually strong official conclusion
attribution_tiers.assessed: a named government or forensic team attributed

method.date_rule: earliest source-supported activity or discovery date; month/year precision preserved
method.vendor_rule: vendor names identify products observed in the affected environment, not proof the vendor caused the compromise
method.attack_rule: ATT&CK mappings restricted to techniques observed or directly supported; plausible techniques labelled analytical hypotheses
method.eurepoc_screen: 175 rows with an energy receiver tag in EuRepoC v1.3; 134 lacked a coded initial-access method; a discovery pool, not 175 technical case studies

boundaries.crossing: phishing, stolen accounts, token/session compromise, vulnerable internet-facing applications
boundaries.control: phishing-resistant MFA, conditional access, session monitoring, privileged access separation

boundaries.crossing: shared VPN, exposed gateway, unmanaged supplier accounts, remote desktop
boundaries.control: inventory every path, time-bound access, unique accounts, MFA, jump hosts, recording and isolation

boundaries.crossing: historian replication, file transfer, engineering workstation, poorly segmented routes
boundaries.control: enforced conduits, protocol allowlists, separate identity, monitored data flows, emergency disconnect

boundaries.crossing: exposed RTU/HMI/router/inverter, cellular APN, weak/default credentials
boundaries.control: eliminate internet exposure, change defaults, signed configuration, device backups, out-of-band recovery

boundaries.crossing: SIS engineering channel or protection-relay programming
boundaries.control: independent safety design, key-switch control, change authorization, logic comparison, physical validation

boundaries.crossing: satellite terminal, cloud region, managed host, UPS/BMS
boundaries.control: dependency map, manual fallback, alternative communications, recovery exercises

subsectors.defense: OT segmentation; independent local control; restore tested with operators

subsectors.defense: protocol-aware monitoring; device configuration baselines; remote access control

subsectors.technology: inverters, RTUs, aggregation gateways, cellular/satellite links, cloud fleet management
subsectors.failure_mode: lost telemetry/control, mass configuration change, supplier compromise
subsectors.defense: fleet asset inventory; signed updates; per-site segmentation; alternate telemetry

subsectors.technology: pipeline SCADA, compressor/pump controls, tank loading, trading/dispatch, SIS
subsectors.failure_mode: business-system shutdown, loading disruption, safety-system manipulation
subsectors.defense: IT/OT separation; manual dispatch; SIS independence; vendor access governance

subsectors.technology: administrative IT, engineering and plant control/safety domains
subsectors.failure_mode: espionage or malware in administrative network; risk of cross-domain movement
subsectors.defense: strict separation, removable-media controls, verified transfer and monitoring

subsectors.technology: ETRM, market APIs, customer and payment systems
subsectors.failure_mode: data theft, fraud, scheduling and billing disruption

cases.name: Ukraine distribution grid, December 2015
cases.entry: spear-phishing macro documents months before; stolen credentials; business IT to control-system VPNs
cases.effect: operator HMIs used to open breakers at multiple substations; destructive actions and telephone DoS impeded recovery; ~225,000 customers, 1-6 hours

attribution.actor: Sandworm (per later US indictment); report cites CISA case study

caveats: BlackEnergy3 was present but did not itself open breakers; operators' remote-control functions were abused
equipment vendors for every substation not established in the public report

cases.name: Ukraine Kyiv-area substation, December 2016 (Industroyer/CrashOverride)
cases.entry: earliest intrusion steps incompletely evidenced (MITRE)
cases.effect: modules for IEC 60870-5-104 and other protocols issued valid commands to RTUs and breakers from a Windows host inside OT; Siemens relay DoS module; wiper; localized blackout at Pivnichna

attribution.actor: Sandworm / GRU Unit 74455 (MITRE reconstruction)

caveats: incomplete evidence about earliest intrusion

cases.name: Saudi petrochemical facility, 2017 (TRITON/TRISIS)
cases.entry: engineering workstation; external entry path not public
cases.effect: attempt to alter logic on Schneider Electric Triconex SIS; safety system tripped

attribution.actor: not named in this report's case text; Dragos analysis cited

caveats: Dragos: original malware did not rely on an inherent Schneider product vulnerability
precise plant not public

cases.name: Kudankulam nuclear plant, India, 2019
cases.entry: unresolved
cases.effect: malware on an internet-connected administrative PC; control and instrumentation systems unaffected and separated (Department of Atomic Energy)

attribution.actor: Dtrack / Lazarus-related per researchers; official source did not establish attribution

caveats: distinction between confirmed IT infection and unconfirmed OT compromise is essential
data exfiltration unresolved

cases.name: Colonial Pipeline, United States, May 2021
cases.case_type: confirmed intrusion (IT) with precautionary OT shutdown
cases.entry: compromised legacy VPN account without MFA (company testimony)
cases.effect: ransomware on IT; CISA/FBI: no indication OT directly affected; operator halted the pipeline to contain risk; widespread fuel-distribution effects
cases.ot_reach: none (IT only); operational shutdown by decision

attribution.actor: DarkSide ransomware (criminal)

caveats: causal chain is IT ransomware to precautionary shutdown, not demonstrated malicious pipeline-control commands

cases.name: KA-SAT/Viasat and German wind farms, February 2022
cases.entry: misconfigured Viasat VPN appliance; trusted management segment; legitimate management commands overwrote modem flash (AcidRain)
cases.effect: German wind-turbine operators lost remote monitoring; generation continued; CERT-EU: likely collateral

attribution.actor: attributed by EU/UK/US to Russia (not restated in case text)

caveats: communications dependency incident, not intrusion into turbine controllers
Viasat: no evidence the firmware-update channel or satellite was compromised

cases.name: Ukraine high-voltage utility, April 2022 (Industroyer2 thwarted)
cases.entry: not stated
cases.effect: Industroyer2 and CaddyWiper deployed; intended outage did not materialize

attribution.actor: Sandworm (CERT-UA, ESET)

caveats: attempted OT disruption with confirmed malware and defensive intervention

cases.name: Danish energy companies, May 2023 (Zyxel firewall exploitation)
cases.entry: crafted UDP/500 IKE packets exploiting CVE-2023-28771 in Zyxel firewalls; later CVE-2023-33009/33010
cases.effect: 11 of 16 targeted organizations initially compromised; firewall configs and account details taken; some devices joined Mirai; one operator lost visibility of three remote sites; no national outage
cases.ot_reach: loss of view at one operator

attribution.actor: SektorCERT saw similarities to Sandworm but did not confirm

caveats: one coordinated campaign in two waves against 22 organizations; do not multiply into 22 cases

cases.name: Ukrainian district heating, January 2024 (FrostyGoop/BUSTLEBERM)
cases.entry: internet-exposed ENCO controllers
cases.effect: Modbus TCP commands; heat disrupted to 600+ apartment buildings; nearly two days to restore

attribution.actor: unknown; malware-to-event linkage at Dragos's moderate confidence

caveats: retain Dragos's confidence qualification

cases.name: Halliburton, United States, August 2024
cases.entry: not established in filings
cases.effect: unauthorized access disclosed 21 August; systems taken offline; data exfiltration reported in SEC filing

attribution.actor: RansomHub claimed in reporting; not confirmed by operator

caveats: claim and confirmed attribution kept separate

cases.name: Nova Scotia Power, Canada, March-April 2025
cases.entry: employee clicked a malicious website pop-up (~19 March) installing SocGholish/FakeUpdates; credential harvesting; domain-admin access
cases.effect: data theft from on-premises and cloud; backups destroyed; ransomware late April; generation, transmission and distribution continued; smart-meter reads and billing disrupted

attribution.actor: not established in the regulator's findings

caveats: no remote meter-disconnect attack established
sources: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada findings

cases.name: Poland distributed energy and CHP, December 2025
cases.entry: compromised edge and remote-access infrastructure; privileged accounts; at a second CHP a misconfigured private APN allowed peer access
cases.effect: 30+ wind and PV farms: RTUs, protection relays and HMIs damaged, loss of communications with DSOs while generation continued; EDR blocked a wiper at a large CHP; at a smaller CHP a steam turbine and process-water treatment stopped briefly, heat continued

attribution.actor: CERT Polska cluster attribution; later UK/EU political attribution recorded separately

caveats: named products (Fortinet edge, Mikronika RTUs/HMIs, Hitachi Relion relays, Moxa NPort) identify affected equipment, not product defects

cases.name: Natanz, Iran, discovered 2010 (Stuxnet)
cases.entry: removable media and Siemens Step 7 project workflows; first infection path not proven publicly
cases.effect: malicious PLC code on SIMATIC S7-315 altered centrifuge-drive behaviour while disguising changes

attribution.actor: US-Israel sponsorship remains reporting, not an official admission

caveats: product naming is not an allegation that suppliers participated

cases.name: Saudi Aramco, August 2012 (Shamoon/Disttrack)
cases.entry: not established
cases.effect: ~30,000 corporate Windows systems destroyed (US DOJ); oil and gas flow not interrupted

attribution.actor: 'Cutting Sword of Justice' claimed; state attribution recorded separately

cases.name: Chornobyl decommissioning site, June 2017 (NotPetya collateral)
cases.entry: site-specific path not public
cases.effect: loss of website, email, file sharing; some radiation-monitoring operator workstations affected; instrument-based monitoring continued; no abnormal radiation

attribution.actor: NotPetya attributed to Russian GRU by US authorities

caveats: not evidence of reactor or safety-system manipulation

cases.name: Bapco, Bahrain, December 2019 (Dustman)
cases.entry: likely VPN appliance exploitation (Kaspersky ICS CERT); domain and service accounts
cases.effect: wiper distributed via antivirus console and PsExec; EldoS RawDisk driver; some machines infected; operations continued

attribution.actor: not stated

caveats: Dustman related to ZeroCleare but not the same

cases.name: RECOPE, Costa Rica, November 2024
cases.entry: not stated
cases.effect: ransomware on administrative systems; SIG/SAP isolated; fuel sales moved to manual after SAP and SVFA billing at land and aviation terminals became unavailable

attribution.actor: not stated

caveats: SAP is the named platform, not an identified exploit or responsible party

cases.name: sPower, United States, March 2019
cases.entry: internet-reachable Cisco firewall vulnerability (DoS)
cases.effect: repeated reboots of devices linking the control centre to twelve remote sites; brief communications loss; output continued; no deeper intrusion found

attribution.actor: not stated

caveats: perimeter-device availability failure, not inverter or turbine manipulation

cases.name: Ukraine utility, October 2022 (MicroSCADA native command abuse)
cases.entry: ISO image with VBScript and batch files on a MicroSCADA server
cases.effect: legitimate scilc.exe invoked to issue unauthorized commands likely opening breakers; unscheduled outage; CaddyWiper later on enterprise systems

attribution.actor: Sandworm (Mandiant)

caveats: some OT command bytes unrecovered; exact command list not established

cases.name: Aliquippa water booster station, United States, November 2023 (Unitronics)
cases.entry: internet-exposed Unitronics Vision PLC/HMI, default passwords over TCP 20256
cases.effect: HMI defacement; booster station placed in manual

attribution.actor: IRGC-affiliated CyberAv3ngers (CISA/partner advisory AA23-335A)

caveats: CISA discusses a product CVE but default credentials are the supported mechanism

trends: Remote access is the recurring pivot (Ukrainian control VPNs, Colonial's legacy VPN, Viasat's appliance, Danish Zyxel firewalls, Poland's edge/private APN): a pattern in the selected cases, not a measured prevalence.
OT effect is rarer in the public record than IT compromise, but harder to recover; a lost remote view can be consequential without a generation outage.
Distributed assets magnify shared mistakes: one upstream compromise, dozens of downstream effects.
Attribution remains separate from impact: outage can be confirmed while actor is only assessed; a claim can exist with no verified effect.

attack_mapping.evidence: Ukraine 2015 control VPN; Poland 2025 edge/VPN path
attack_mapping.emphasis: inventory access, MFA, unique accounts, source restrictions, session recording

attack_mapping.evidence: Ukraine 2015 HMI; Triton OT jump path; Poland 2025 SSH/RDP/SMB
attack_mapping.emphasis: monitor cross-zone sessions; restrict jump-host protocol and time window

attack_mapping.evidence: Poland 2025 privileged/default accounts; Ukraine 2015 stolen credentials
attack_mapping.emphasis: rotate credentials; remove defaults; device-specific identities

attack_mapping.evidence: Ukraine 2015 breakers; Ukraine 2016 protocol commands; FrostyGoop Modbus
attack_mapping.emphasis: correlate control commands with operator authorization and process state

attack_mapping.evidence: Industroyer wiper modules; Poland 2025 RTU/HMI destruction
attack_mapping.emphasis: offline/signed images; recovery rehearsal; engineering workstation monitoring

attack_mapping.technique: T0827 Loss of Control / T0829 Loss of View
attack_mapping.evidence: Poland 2025 severed DSO remote control and telemetry
attack_mapping.emphasis: independent local control, out-of-band telemetry, safety procedures

attack_mapping.technique: T1693.001 Modify Firmware / T1694.001 Default Credentials
attack_mapping.emphasis: firmware baselines, credential reset, managed lifecycle

defensive_program: Map critical services to real asset dependencies (plant controller, RTU, relay, modem, satellite link, APN, identity provider, data centre, contractor); record technical and recovery owners; NIST SP 800-82.
Close direct internet exposure of OT; private connectivity, phishing-resistant MFA, least privilege, monitored jump paths (CISA OT mitigation guidance).
Treat vendor access and IT/OT conduits as controlled production changes; verify inventory, ownership, patch responsibility, product version and emergency revocation per supplier.
OT-aware monitoring of engineering changes, control commands, relay settings, reboots, firmware updates, loss of view; pair cyber alerts with process alarms and operator confirmation.

Recovery independent of compromised IT: immutable backups of identity, historian, HMI and engineering projects; signed firmware and relay settings; spare field devices; local procedures; tested manual dispatch and communications.
Govern with DOE C2M2 and applicable requirements; check the currently enforceable NERC CIP version.
exclusions: Oldsmar 2021 water-treatment story: challenged by later FBI-related reporting; not a confirmed compromise
2007 California canal SCADA indictment: dismissed; not proven sabotage
2025 Norwegian Bremanger/Risevatnet dam: aquaculture water supply, not verified hydropower
2025 Iberian blackout: not a cyberattack per the official investigation
Denmark 2023 and Poland 2025: one campaign each, not one case per site
